analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing wages for service workers on federal contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Service Contract Act was referred to a House subcommittee and died there without a hearing or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Service Contract Act of 1965 requires companies that win federal service contracts — such as janitorial, food service, and security work — to pay their workers wages and benefits set by the Department of Labor. This bill would have repealed that law entirely, letting those companies set pay at whatever the market allowed. It was introduced by Rep. George Allen with six Republican cosponsors and died in a House subcommittee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies holding or bidding on federal service contracts would gain, since they could pay wages below the current government-set minimums. Larger federal contractors with many low-wage service employees would see the biggest savings.

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the Service Contract Act would free companies holding federal service contracts from the requirement to pay contractually set prevailing wages and benefits to their employees.
The bill grandfathers existing contracts, applying the Act only to contracts entered into before enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly hundreds of thousands of low-wage workers on federal service contracts — janitors, food service workers, security guards — would bear the cost, as the law currently sets a wage and benefit floor that would disappear.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the federal wage floor that the Service Contract Act sets for low-wage service workers on federal contracts, leaving those workers' pay to whatever the market or contract bids produce.
The bill received no committee hearing or vote in the roughly two months before the Congress ended, so its impact was limited to the referral stage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit would be lower federal contract costs and less paperwork for service firms; the cost would be lower wages and benefits for the roughly hundreds of thousands of low-wage janitors, guards, and other service workers whose pay the Act currently protects, who would likely see wages drift down when contracts change hands.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to a House subcommittee that never acted on it, and the session ended with no hearing, vote, or further movement.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 1992, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On August 25, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where no further action followed.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, with the bill still stuck in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal service contractors who would have benefited from paying lower wages kept the current law; low-wage service workers kept their wage protections. House Republican leaders on the Labor Committee effectively buried a bill they did not advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage federal service workers kept protections

for.name: Rep. George Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Service Contract Act.

for.name: Reps. Rohrabacher, Dannemeyer, Smith of Texas, Coble, and Boehner
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the repeal bill.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Labor Standards
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 25, 1992, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled House committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: Government service contractors and their low-wage workers
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the legal requirement that federal service contractors pay employees prevailing wages and benefits, a protection that mainly benefits lower-paid janitors, guards, food service, and maintenance workers.

industries.industry: Federal service contractors (janitorial, food, security, maintenance firms)
industries.note: Repeal would let these firms bid on and profit from federal contracts without a mandated wage and benefit floor, lowering labor costs at workers' expense.
